title: AI Is Redefining Entry-Level Work Around Judgment
summary: New Upwork research shows that AI may not be eliminating entry-level work, but it is changing what it takes to succeed.
body_markdown:
by Jennifer Brett


### Key Insights


- **More automation does not necessarily mean fewer entry-level roles.** Advanced organizations are more likely than foundational organizations to automate coding, testing, or troubleshooting - 57% versus 34% - and to report that AI has increased entry-level hiring: 57% versus 17%.
- **AI maturity raises the entry-level bar.** Nearly all advanced organizations require AI skills for at least some entry-level roles (98%), while 53% expect candidates to integrate AI into workflows and 44% seek AI-building or configuration skills.
- **Judgment is becoming a core entry-level skill.** As AI takes on drafting, research, analysis, and other foundational tasks, 57% of organizations expect entry-level talent to evaluate AI output for accuracy and quality. Success increasingly depends on knowing how to assess, improve, and apply what AI produces.


## As AI use matures, entry-level success depends on applying judgment, not just using the tools.


AI may not be eliminating entry-level work, but it is changing what it takes to succeed.


Among 750 U.S. business leaders surveyed by the Upwork Research Institute, **42% say AI has increased entry-level hiring over the past year. Another 49% say hiring has remained stable, but the roles or required skills have changed. Only 5% report a decrease due to AI.**


This suggests that the focus needs to shift from whether entry-level jobs will remain to what people will be expected to do in them, and how they need to prepare.


AI is increasingly handling the foundational tasks on which many careers once began, including data processing, first drafts, summarization, basic research, and elements of coding and testing. Entry-level employees may now begin with an AI-generated output rather than a blank page.


That shifts their contribution from producing routine work to evaluating it, improving it, applying it to the business context, and recognizing when it cannot be trusted.


This change is visible across organizations, but the skills expected of entry-level talent evolve as organizations become more mature in how they use AI. Basic AI fluency is becoming a minimum expectation. More advanced organizations increasingly expect new hires to integrate AI into workflows, use it responsibly, and help turn the technology into business results.


## AI maturity changes the entry-level model


The Upwork Research Institute assessed organizations across five elements of AI operating maturity: deployment, business outcomes, measurement, workflow redesign, and structured orchestration. Organizations were then classified as foundational, developing, or advanced.


The results reveal a striking pattern: **greater AI maturity is associated with more entry-level hiring due to AI, not less.** Even though AI has not increased entry-level hiring at most foundational organizations, entry-level roles and required skills are changing there too.


**Table 1: Entry-level hiring and skills by AI operating maturity level**


The question for employers is shifting from “Do we still need entry-level workers?” to “What should entry-level workers contribute to an AI-enabled organization?”


## Tasks are being automated. Roles are evolving.


AI is already taking on work historically associated with entry-level roles. According to the business leaders surveyed:


- 70% of organizations automate data entry, processing, or basic analysis.
- 64% automate the drafting of emails, documents, or presentations.
- 60% automate summarization.
- 59% automate basic research and information gathering.
- 48% automate elements of coding, testing, or technical troubleshooting.


Advanced organizations tend to automate more of this work. For example, 57% automate coding, testing, or technical troubleshooting, compared with 34% of foundational organizations.


Yet advanced organizations are also the most likely to report an increase in entry-level hiring. This shows why tasks and jobs should not be treated as interchangeable. **Automating individual activities can change a role without eliminating the need for the person performing it** .


An entry-level employee who once gathered information, completed a basic analysis, or produced a first draft may now begin with an AI-generated output. Their contribution increasingly comes from[evaluating it, improving it,](https://wf-resources.upwork.com/research/ai-generated-work-is-creating-more-work-for-humans) applying it to the business context, and recognizing when it cannot be trusted.


## AI fluency is the new starting point. Judgment is the differentiator.


AI skills are now required for at least some entry-level roles at 86% of surveyed organizations, and 96% assess AI capabilities during hiring.


Employers are not looking only for technical specialists. Their most common expectations combine practical tool use with human judgment: using role-specific AI tools, evaluating output for accuracy and quality, prompting effectively, and improving AI-generated work.


Those expectations become more sophisticated as organizations mature. **Foundational organizations place greater emphasis on basic tool use, prompting, and editing. Advanced organizations are more likely to prioritize responsible AI use, workflow integration, and the ability to build or configure AI solutions** .


For example, 53% of advanced organizations expect or prefer entry-level candidates to integrate AI tools into workflows, compared with 36% of foundational organizations. Forty-four percent of advanced organizations seek AI-building or configuration skills, twice the foundational share.


The challenge is that employees have traditionally developed judgment by performing the repeatable, lower-risk tasks AI increasingly handles. Employers must now redesign not only entry-level roles, but also how people learn within them.


Entry-level talent still needs opportunities to understand how decisions are made, identify risks, and determine when human intervention is required. AI fluency may help candidates enter the workforce; judgment can help them contribute and advance.


## Freelance talent can help build the bridge


Freelance talent can support this transition in two ways.


First, experienced freelancers can help organizations[implement AI](https://www.upwork.com/research/ai-orchestration-is-a-team-effort) , design workflows, establish quality standards, and transfer specialized knowledge to internal teams. This gives organizations access to capabilities they may not yet have in-house while preparing employees to operate those systems over time.


Second, freelance and project-based work can help emerging professionals build portfolios and demonstrate the skills employers increasingly expect. Completed projects offer evidence that someone can use AI responsibly, assess its output, and apply it to a real business problem. Based on previous Upwork Research Institute research, AI could be influencing younger workers to pursue this path: 67% of Gen Z working full-time are considering freelancing in 2026 to better access professional opportunities around them, up from 51% in 2025 (source: survey of 421 Gen Z U.S.-based workers conducted from March to April 2026).


Freelancers are therefore not a substitute for entry-level talent. Flexible experts can help organizations build AI-enabled systems, while project-based work can help the next generation of workers develop the experience needed to participate in them.


## The career ladder is changing, not disappearing


The findings do not suggest that AI will leave entry-level work unchanged. Routine tasks are being automated, skill expectations are rising, and organizations will need new ways to develop judgment and expertise.


**But the defining entry-level skill in an AI-enabled organization will not be the ability to produce more output with a new tool. It will be the ability to determine whether that output is accurate, useful, responsible, and relevant to the problem at hand** .


As organizations become more mature in their use of AI, they will need entry-level talent that can connect tools to workflows, outputs to decisions, and automation to business results. AI fluency may help someone enter the workforce, but human skills, like judgment, will determine how they contribute and advance.


## Methodology


The data is based on a survey of 750 U.S.-based business leaders (director plus seniority) from August to September 2026. The survey was fielded externally by McGuire Research.


The Upwork AI Operating Maturity Model measures organizations’ progress from isolated AI adoption to scaled, outcome-oriented operating transformation. We define AI operating maturity based on capability thresholds that we have established across five organizational dimensions: breadth of deployment, clarity of business outcomes, measurement, workflow redesign, and structured orchestration. Organizations meeting zero or one of these thresholds are classified as foundational, those meeting two or three as developing, and those meeting four or five as advanced. Its five dimensions reflect capabilities identified in established AI maturity, governance, and value-realization frameworks (such as[Microsoft](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agents/adoption-maturity-model/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) ,[McKinsey](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-state-of-ai-how-organizations-are-rewiring-to-capture-value?utm_source=chatgpt.com) , and[NIST](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.100-1.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com) ). The model is designed as a concise, survey-based operating index rather than a comprehensive assessment of every element of AI readiness.


Basic AI adoption is already high across all three segments. Even among foundational organizations, 88% report using AI regularly somewhere in the business. This indicates that the AI operating maturity model is reflective of how AI is utilized within an organization after basic adoption.


AI operating maturity does not rise consistently with company size. Very large organizations are most likely to be advanced, but very small organizations also perform strongly. This suggests that resources and scale can help, but they are not prerequisites for maturity. Organizational focus, agility, workflow redesign, and clear ownership may matter as much as employee count.

### About The Upwork Research Institute


The world of work is not the same as it was just a few years ago, and leaders are facing new challenges as a result. The old work playbook is gone, and in its place are new debates and decisions around workforce location, worker arrangements, flexibility, and the role of AI in how work gets done. Leaders do not need to navigate this new world of work on their own.


The Upwork Research Institute is committed to studying the fundamental shifts in the workforce and providing business leaders with the tools and insights they need to navigate the here and now while preparing their organizations for the future. Using proprietary platform data, global survey research, partnerships, and academic collaborations, the Institute produces evidence-based insights to help create the blueprint for the new way of work.


### About the author


[Jennifer Brett](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jennifermbrett/) is the managing director of The Upwork Research Institute, where she leads research and thought leadership on the future of work, including AI, flexible talent, and evolving workforce models. She is a research and insights leader with more than 15 years of experience translating data, market signals, and human behavior into strategies, narratives, and business impact. Jennifer has held senior insights leadership roles at Attentive and LinkedIn across the U.S. and Europe, and previously served as an industry analyst at Google. She holds a Ph.D. in political science from Trinity College Dublin, with academic training in research design and quantitative and qualitative methods.
